title: The imperative: instructions and recipes
objectives: I can form the imperative for 'ти', 'ви' and 'ми' from the present stem, choosing between '-й', '-и' and no ending.
I can use the irregular imperatives 'їж', 'пий', 'дай' and 'будь', and I know that 'ви́бачте', 'бува́й' and 'будь ла́ска' contain imperatives.
I can choose the aspect of an imperative: perfective for one specific act, imperfective for advice, invitations and commands with 'не'.
I can propose doing something together with 'дава́й' and 'дава́йте', and say what someone else should do with 'неха́й'.
I can follow and give the steps of a recipe, naming vegetables, ingredients and kitchen things.

vocabulary.note: 'Варю́', 'ва́риш'. Perfective 'звари́ти'. It means to cook in boiling water, as soup, potatoes and varenyky are cooked; the word 'варе́ники' comes from it. With '-ся', 'вари́тися' says that the food is cooking: 'Борщ ва́риться.', the borscht is cooking.

example.target: Ма́ма ва́рить борщ у вели́кій кастру́лі.
example.source: Mom is cooking borscht in a big saucepan.

vocabulary.note: 'Сма́жу', 'сма́жиш'. Perfective 'посма́жити'. Food is fried 'на олі́ї', literally 'on oil'.
'Рі́жу', 'рі́жеш', 'рі́жуть': the 'з' becomes 'ж' in every present form. Perfective 'порі́зати', to cut up.
Built from 'да́ти' and conjugated like it: 'дода́м', 'додаси́', 'дода́сть', 'додаду́ть'. Imperfective 'додава́ти' ('додаю́', 'додає́ш').

example.source: Oksana mixed the flour and water.

vocabulary.note: 'Ми́ю', 'ми́єш'. Perfective 'поми́ти'. Used for washing hands, dishes, vegetables and the floor.
Like 'карто́пля', used in the singular for onion as food.

example.source: The onion is already on the table.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'часнику́': a substance takes '-у', and the stress moves to the ending.

example.source: You need to add garlic to the borscht.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'буряка́', with the stress on the ending. Beets give borscht its red color.

example.target: Борщ черво́ний, бо в ньо́му є буря́к.
example.source: Borscht is red because there is beet in it.
example.source_literal: Borscht red, because in it is beet.

vocabulary.note: Like 'карто́пля', used in the singular for carrots as food.

example.target: Мо́рква й цибу́ля вже в кастру́лі.
example.source: The carrots and onion are already in the saucepan.

vocabulary.note: Vegetable oil for cooking and salads, in Ukraine usually sunflower oil. Locative 'на олі́ї'.

example.target: Де олі́я? Вона́ там, бі́ля вікна́.
example.source: Where's the oil? It's over there, by the window.

vocabulary.note: Plural 'я́йця', with the stress on the first syllable.

example.target: Ура́нці я їм яйце́ й хліб.
example.source: In the morning I eat an egg and bread.

vocabulary.note: A mass noun, used only in the singular.

example.target: Ми ку́пимо бо́рошно й цу́кор у магази́ні.
example.source: We'll buy flour and sugar at the shop.

vocabulary.note: A deep pot for soup and for boiling. Locative 'у кастру́лі'.

A word for an amount takes the genitive of what is measured: 'ло́жка цу́кру', a spoon of sugar; 'скля́нка води́', a glass of water; 'тро́хи со́лі', a little salt; 'Скі́льки води́?', how much water? With the instrumental it is the tool: 'зміша́ти ло́жкою', to mix with a spoon.
The 'ти' imperative of 'дава́ти', to give, used to propose doing something together. 'Дава́йте' is said to someone you call 'ви' or to a group.
Also 'хай', shorter and more conversational. With the 'він', 'вона́' or 'вони́' form of a verb it says what someone else should do, or what you wish to happen.

example.source: Let the children go for a walk in the park.

dialogues.title: Borscht with Halyna
dialogues.context: Sam is visiting Oksana's parents, and her mother Halyna is teaching him to cook borscht. Sam says 'ви' to Halyna and calls her 'па́ні Гали́но'; she says 'ти' to him, as an older person often does to a young friend of the family.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Се́ме, сього́дні ти бу́деш вари́ти борщ, а я бу́ду допомага́ти.
lines.source: Sam, today you're going to cook the borscht, and I'll help.
lines.source_literal: Sam, today you will to-cook borscht, and I will to-help.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре, па́ні Гали́но. Що тре́ба зроби́ти споча́тку?
lines.source: All right, Ms. Halyna. What do I need to do first?
lines.source_literal: Good, Ms. Halyna. What necessary to-do first?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: М’я́со вже в кастру́лі. Поми́й буря́к, мо́ркву й карто́плю.
lines.source: The meat is already in the saucepan. Wash the beet, the carrots and the potatoes.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я вже їх поми́в. А що по́тім?
lines.source: I've already washed them. What comes next?
lines.source_literal: I already them washed. And what then?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Порі́ж цибу́лю, мо́ркву й буря́к. Ріж пові́льно!
lines.source: Cut up the onion, the carrots and the beet. Cut slowly!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А капу́сту теж?
lines.source: And the cabbage too?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Ні, капу́сту по́тім. За́раз візьми́ олі́ю й посма́ж їх.
lines.source: No, the cabbage comes later. Now take the oil and fry them.
lines.source_literal: No, cabbage then. Now take oil and fry them.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Скі́льки хвили́н?
lines.source: For how many minutes?
lines.source_literal: How-many of-minutes?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: П’ять хвили́н. Не смаж їх до́вго.
lines.source: Five minutes. Don't fry them for long.
lines.source_literal: Five of-minutes. Not fry them long.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я все посма́жив.
lines.source: I've fried everything.
lines.source_literal: I everything fried.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Дода́й у кастру́лю карто́плю й капу́сту, а по́тім буря́к, мо́ркву й цибу́лю.
lines.source: Add the potatoes and cabbage to the saucepan, and then the beet, carrots and onion.
lines.source_literal: Add into saucepan potatoes and cabbage, and then beet, carrots and onion.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А сіль і часни́к?
lines.source: And the salt and garlic?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Сіль дода́й за́раз, а часни́к по́тім. Неха́й борщ ва́риться ще де́сять хвили́н.
lines.source: Add the salt now and the garlic later. Let the borscht cook for ten more minutes.
lines.source_literal: Salt add now, and garlic then. Let borscht cooks more ten of-minutes.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дава́йте я за́раз зроблю́ сала́т.
lines.source: Let me make a salad now.
lines.source_literal: Let's I now will-make salad.

dialogues.title: Varenyky for the family
dialogues.context: Taras and his sister Olena are making varenyky with potatoes for a family dinner. Brother and sister say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Тара́се, дава́й зро́бимо варе́ники з карто́плею.
lines.source: Taras, let's make varenyky with potatoes.
lines.source_literal: Taras, let's will-make varenyky with potatoes.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Дава́й! Карто́плю я вже звари́в.
lines.source: Let's! I've already boiled the potatoes.
lines.source_literal: Let's! Potatoes I already boiled.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: До́бре. За́раз порі́ж цибу́лю й посма́ж її́ на олі́ї.
lines.source: Good. Now cut up the onion and fry it in oil.
lines.source_literal: Good. Now cut-up onion and fry it on oil.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А ти що бу́деш роби́ти?
lines.source: And what are you going to do?
lines.source_literal: And you what will to-do?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Я зміша́ю бо́рошно, яйце́ й во́ду.
lines.source: I'll mix the flour, an egg and water.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ось бо́рошно. Скі́льки води́?
lines.source: Here's the flour. How much water?
lines.source_literal: Here flour. How-much of-water?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Одну́ скля́нку. Дай мені́, будь ла́ска, ло́жку.
lines.source: One glass. Give me a spoon, please.
lines.source_literal: One glass. Give to-me, please, spoon.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Цю?
lines.source: This one?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ні, не бери́ цю, вона́ мала́. Візьми́ вели́ку.
lines.source: No, don't take this one, it's small. Take the big one.
lines.source_literal: No, not take this, it small. Take big.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ось. А цибу́лю я вже посма́жив.
lines.source: Here you are. And I've already fried the onion.
lines.source_literal: Here. And onion I already fried.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Зміша́й її́ з карто́плею й дода́й тро́хи со́лі.
lines.source: Mix it with the potatoes and add a little salt.
lines.source_literal: Mix it with potatoes and add a-little of-salt.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Слу́хай, а хто бу́де ї́сти всі ці варе́ники?
lines.source: Listen, who's going to eat all these varenyky?
lines.source_literal: Listen, and who will to-eat all these varenyky?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: На́ша сім’я́! Хай та́то ку́пить смета́ну.
lines.source: Our family! Let Dad buy the sour cream.
lines.source_literal: Our family! Let dad will-buy sour-cream.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ні, ході́мо в магази́н ра́зом, коли́ закі́нчимо.
lines.source: No, let's go to the shop together when we're done.
lines.source_literal: No, let's-go to shop together, when we-will-finish.

dialogues.title: A new waiter
dialogues.context: It is Bohdan's first morning as a waiter at Andrii's café, and Andrii, the owner, explains the work. They say 'ви' to each other, as people often do at work when they have just met.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Богда́не, до́брий ра́нок! Сього́дні у вас пе́рший день.
lines.source: Good morning, Bohdan! Today is your first day.
lines.source_literal: Bohdan, good morning! Today at you first day.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий ра́нок, па́не Андрі́ю. Що тре́ба роби́ти?
lines.source: Good morning, Mr. Andrii. What do I need to do?
lines.source_literal: Good morning, Mr. Andrii. What necessary to-do?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Споча́тку поми́йте ча́шки й скля́нки. Ми́йте їх шви́дко, але́ до́бре.
lines.source: First wash the cups and glasses. Wash them quickly, but well.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́бре. Що ще?
lines.source: All right. What else?
lines.source_literal: Good. What more?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: По́тім порі́жте хліб і сир. Рі́жте їх тут, а не на столі́.
lines.source: Then cut the bread and cheese. Cut them here, not on the table.
lines.source_literal: Then cut-up bread and cheese. Cut them here, and not on table.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: А якщо́ хтось хо́че ка́ву?
lines.source: And if someone wants coffee?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Ка́ву роблю́ я, а ви да́йте меню́ й скажі́ть: «До́брий день!»
lines.source: I make the coffee, and you give them the menu and say 'Hello!'
lines.source_literal: Coffee make I, and you give menu and say: «Good day!»

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: А раху́нок?
lines.source: And the bill?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Раху́нок дава́йте пі́сля ка́ви. Неха́й вони́ відпочива́ють.
lines.source: Give them the bill after the coffee. Let them relax.
lines.source_literal: Bill give after coffee. Let they rest.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́бре, дя́кую.
lines.source: All right, thank you.
lines.source_literal: Good, I-thank.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: І ще одне́: завжди́ кажі́ть «будь ла́ска» й «дя́кую».
lines.source: And one more thing: always say 'please' and 'thank you'.
lines.source_literal: And more one: always say «be kindness» and «I-thank».

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Звича́йно, па́не Андрі́ю.
lines.source: Of course, Mr. Andrii.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: А за́раз бері́ть ча́шку й пи́йте ка́ву, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: And now please take a cup and have some coffee.
lines.source_literal: And now take cup and drink coffee, please.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Дя́кую!
lines.source: Thank you!
lines.source_literal: I-thank!

grammar.title: The imperative: three forms built on the present stem
grammar.explanation:
The imperative is the verb form that tells someone to do something: an instruction, a request, advice or an invitation. English uses the bare verb for this ('Read!', 'Add the salt.'), the same for one person or many. Ukrainian has three forms: one for a person you call 'ти', one for 'ви', which serves a person you call 'ви' and any group, and one for 'ми', meaning 'let's'.

Nearly every imperative is built on the present stem, and the next note gives the few that are not. The stem is the 'вони́' form without its ending '-уть', '-ють', '-ать' or '-ять'. A perfective verb has no present, so its future 'вони́' form is used in the same way ('зміша́ють', 'ста́нуть'). What comes next depends on how the stem ends and where the 'я' form has its stress:

- After a vowel, the stem ends in the sound [j], which '-ють' and '-ять' hide inside their first letter: 'чита́ють' is [t͡ʃɪˈtɑjutʲ]. The imperative ends in this sound, written 'й': 'чита́й', 'працю́й', 'зміша́й', 'мий'.
- After a consonant, when the 'я' form is stressed on the ending, add a stressed '-и': 'пишу́', 'пи́шуть', so 'пиши́'; 'варю́', 'ва́рять', so 'вари́'; 'беру́', 'беру́ть', so 'бери́'.
- After a consonant, when the 'я' form is stressed on the stem, add nothing: 'рі́жу', 'рі́жуть', so 'ріж'; 'сма́жу', 'сма́жать', so 'смаж'; 'ста́ну', 'ста́нуть', so 'стань'.

The form for 'ви' adds '-те' and the form for 'ми' adds '-мо' to a form in '-й' or with no ending: 'чита́йте', 'чита́ймо'; 'рі́жте', 'рі́жмо'; 'ста́ньте', 'ста́ньмо'. After '-и' the 'и' becomes 'і', so the endings are '-іть' and '-імо': 'пиші́ть', 'пиші́мо'; 'варі́ть', 'варі́мо'. The stress stays on the syllable that carries it in the imperative for 'ти'.

Three details complete the rule:

- The 'л' that 'ро́блять', 'лю́блять' and 'ку́плять' add after 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м' and 'ф' belongs only to the 'я' and 'вони́' forms, so the imperative does not have it: 'роби́', 'люби́', 'купи́'.
- When the 'я' form is stressed on the stem and the stem ends in two consonants, '-и' is kept without stress, because two consonants are hard to say at the end of a word: 'закі́нчу', so 'закі́нчи', 'закі́нчіть'.
- A reflexive verb adds '-ся' after the imperative: 'одяга́йся', and for 'ви' 'одяга́йтеся' or 'одяга́йтесь'.

Do not confuse the imperative for 'ви' with the present. 'Ви пи́шете.' means 'You write.', while 'Пиші́ть!' means 'Write!'. The two differ in the ending and often in the stress.

examples.target: Вари́ карто́плю, а я поми́ю мо́ркву.
examples.source: Boil the potatoes, and I'll wash the carrots.

grammar.title: Irregular imperatives, and the ones you already know
grammar.explanation:
A few common verbs build the imperative in their own way. Learn these forms whole:

- 'ї́сти', to eat: 'їж', 'ї́жте', 'ї́жмо'
- 'пи́ти', to drink: 'пий', 'пи́йте', 'пи́ймо'
- 'да́ти', to give: 'дай', 'да́йте', 'да́ймо'
- 'дода́ти', to add, which is built from 'да́ти': 'дода́й', 'дода́йте'
- 'бу́ти', to be: 'будь', 'бу́дьте', 'бу́дьмо'

Verbs that end in '-авати' keep the '-ва-' of the infinitive, although their present has lost it ('даю́ть', 'встаю́ть'): 'дава́ти' gives 'дава́й', 'встава́ти' gives 'встава́й', and 'додава́ти' gives 'додава́й'.

'Іти́' follows the rule of the first note: 'іду́' is stressed on the ending, so the imperative is 'іди́', 'іді́ть'. After a vowel the euphony rule gives 'йди' and 'йдіть': 'Ти йди додо́му, а я ще працю́ю.' (You go home; I am still working.) After a comma the 'і' form stays: 'Окса́но, іди́ сюди́!' (Oksana, come here!) To say 'let's go', Ukrainians use 'ході́мо', which the note on 'let's' explains.

Three expressions you have used since the unit on greetings are imperatives:

- 'ви́бачте', excuse me, is the 'ви' form of 'ви́бачити', to forgive. Its 'я' form 'ви́бачу' is stressed on the stem, so the 'ти' form has no ending: 'ви́бач'.
- 'бува́й', bye, is the 'ти' form of 'бува́ти', to be from time to time. It is shortened from the longer farewell 'бува́й здоро́вий', literally 'be healthy'.
- 'будь ла́ска', please, is 'будь', the 'ти' form of 'бу́ти', with the noun 'ла́ска', kindness: literally 'be kindness'. It has become a fixed phrase and is said to everyone, also to people you call 'ви'. A more formal request to someone you call 'ви' uses 'бу́дьте ла́скаві', literally 'be kind'.

examples.source: Get up, Sam, it's already seven o'clock.

grammar.title: Aspect in the imperative, and politeness
grammar.explanation:
The imperative has both aspects, and the choice follows the meaning of aspect you know: the perfective presents one complete act with a result, and the imperfective presents an action as a process, a habit or simply the action itself. A perfective imperative does not refer to the future. It asks for the act now, or at the time the context sets.

Use the perfective for one specific act that should be done and finished. This is the usual form of a request and of each step in a recipe:

- 'Дода́йте сіль.' (Add the salt.)
- 'Візьми́ ло́жку.' (Take a spoon.)
- 'Купі́ть хліб, будь ла́ска.' (Please buy some bread.)

Use the imperfective in these cases:

- general advice or a habit: 'Чита́йте ча́сто.' (Read often.)
- how to do something, or for how long: 'Ріж пові́льно.' (Cut slowly.), 'Варі́ть суп де́сять хвили́н.' (Boil the soup for ten minutes.)
- an invitation to do what the listener is welcome to do: 'Бері́ть, будь ла́ска.' (Please help yourself.)
- a command with 'не': 'Не сма́жте м’я́со до́вго.' (Don't fry the meat for long.)

The pair 'Візьмі́ть ка́ву.' and 'Бері́ть ка́ву.' shows the difference. The perfective tells someone to take the coffee, perhaps to carry it to a table; the imperfective invites them to help themselves. Hosts say 'бері́ть', 'ї́жте' and 'пи́йте' to their guests, and a perfective in that place would sound like an order.

A perfective with 'не' is used only as a warning against something that could happen by accident: 'Не забу́дь купи́ти хліб!' (Don't forget to buy bread!), from the perfective verb 'забу́ти', to forget.

To make a request polite, add 'будь ла́ска' at the start of the request, at its end, or right after the imperative: 'Да́йте, будь ла́ска, меню́.' (Please give me the menu.) To a person you call 'ви', always use the 'ви' form, because a 'ти' form would sound too familiar.

rows: Boil the soup for ten minutes.
Don't fry the meat for long.

examples.target: Купи́ мо́ркву й цибу́лю, будь ла́ска.
examples.source: Please buy carrots and an onion.

examples.target: Не бери́ цю кастру́лю, вона́ мала́.
examples.source: Don't take this saucepan, it's small.
examples.source_literal: Not take this saucepan, it small.

grammar.title: Let's and let him: дава́й, the 'ми' imperative and неха́й
grammar.explanation:
English proposes a shared action with 'let's'. Ukrainian has two ways to do this, and a third construction says what another person should do.

'Дава́й' is the 'ти' imperative of 'дава́ти', to give, used as a particle that proposes doing something together. Say 'дава́й' to one person you call 'ти', and 'дава́йте' to a person you call 'ви' or to a group. What follows depends on the aspect of the verb:

- an imperfective verb follows in the infinitive: 'Дава́й вари́ти борщ.' (Let's cook borscht.)
- a perfective verb follows in its future 'ми' form, without the word 'ми': 'Дава́йте зро́бимо сала́т.' (Let's make a salad.)

With 'я' and a perfective future, 'дава́й' offers help: 'Дава́йте я поми́ю ча́шки.' (Let me wash the cups.) Said alone, 'Дава́й!' accepts a proposal, like English 'OK, let's!'. 'Дава́йте' can still simply mean 'give', and then it has an object and no second verb: 'Раху́нок дава́йте пі́сля ка́ви.' (Give the bill after the coffee.)

The imperative also has its own form for 'ми', built with '-мо' as the first note showed: 'чита́ймо', let's read; 'зробі́мо', let's make. In everyday speech it is common mainly in 'ході́мо', let's go, from 'ходи́ти', another verb for going on foot: 'Ході́мо в парк!' Other verbs use it in writing, songs and slogans, and in the toast 'Бу́дьмо!', literally 'let's be', said when people raise their glasses.

'Неха́й', or the shorter and more conversational 'хай', goes with the 'він', 'вона́' or 'вони́' form of a verb. It says what someone else should do, or what you wish to happen: 'Неха́й Тара́с ку́пить хліб.' (Let Taras buy the bread, or Taras should buy the bread.) An imperfective verb is in the present, 'Хай вони́ відпочива́ють.' (Let them rest.), and a perfective verb in its future. Ukrainian has no imperative of its own for 'він' or 'вони́', and 'неха́й' does this job. It is a particle, not a verb.

examples.source: Let me cut up the onion.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: ріж, сма́жте, дода́йте, яйце́ and я́йця
grammar.explanation:
Every new form in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The imperative puts consonants at the end of a word and before '-те', and the new nouns bring soft consonants and moving stress.

'Ріж' [rʲiʒ] comes from 'рі́зати'. In every present form the 'з' of the infinitive becomes 'ж' ('рі́жу', 'рі́жеш', 'рі́жуть'), and the imperative is built on that present stem, so it has 'ж' too. The 'я' form is stressed on the stem, so there is no ending. 'Ж' is voiced and stays voiced at the end of the word, as the 'б' of 'хліб' does. It also stays voiced before 'т': 'рі́жте' [ˈrʲiʒtɛ], 'сма́жте' [ˈsmɑʒtɛ]. In general a Ukrainian voiced consonant keeps its voice before a voiceless one, so 'ло́жка' is [ˈlɔʒkɑ] as well; the 'г' of 'могти́', said [x], is one of the few exceptions.

'Дода́йте' [dɔˈdɑjtɛ] has three syllables, because it has three vowel letters. 'Й' is a consonant and closes the second syllable. The same 'й' ends 'чита́й', 'мий' and 'пий', and stands before '-те' and '-мо' in 'чита́йте' and 'ми́ймо'. 'Мий' and 'пий' have one vowel each, so they carry no stress mark.

An imperative with no ending ends in the last consonant of the stem. When that consonant is 'д', 'т', 'з', 'с', 'ц', 'л' or 'н', it is soft, and the soft sign shows it: 'стань' [stɑnʲ], 'будь' [budʲ], and 'їдь' from 'ї́хати', to go by vehicle. The soft sign stays before '-те' and '-мо': 'ста́ньте', 'бу́дьте' [ˈbudʲtɛ], 'бу́дьмо'. 'Ж', 'ч', 'ш' and 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' never take the soft sign: 'ріж', 'смаж', 'ви́бач'.

An imperative in '-и' takes its stress from the 'я' form, not from the present 'ти' form: 'пишу́', 'пиши́', although 'пи́шеш'; 'варю́', 'вари́', although 'ва́риш'. Where '-и' is stressed, the forms for 'ви' and 'ми' keep the stress on the ending: 'пиші́ть', 'варі́мо'. 'Ході́мо' keeps the 'д' of 'ходи́ти', soft before 'і'.

'Ва́риться', from 'вари́тися', ends in '-ться', said [t͡sʲːɑ] as in 'прокида́ється': [ˈʋɑrɪt͡sʲːɑ].

The new nouns:

- 'Яйце́' [jɑjˈt͡sɛ] begins with 'я' said [jɑ], because it is the first letter of the word, and the 'й' after it closes the first syllable. In the plural 'я́йця' [ˈjɑjt͡sʲɑ] the stress moves to the first syllable, as in 'вікно́', 'ві́кна', and 'ц' is soft before 'я'.
- 'Олі́я' [ɔˈlʲijɑ]: 'я' after a vowel is [jɑ], and 'л' is soft before 'і'.
- 'Цибу́ля' and 'кастру́ля' have a soft 'л' before 'я'; 'буря́к' has a soft 'р' before 'я'.
- 'Часни́к' and 'буря́к' move the stress to the ending in their other forms: 'часнику́', 'буряка́'.
- 'Мо́рква' [ˈmɔrkʋɑ]: 'в' before a vowel is [ʋ].
- 'Бо́рошно' [ˈbɔrɔʃnɔ]: all three 'о' keep their full sound, although two of them are unstressed.
- 'Їж' [jiʒ] and 'ї́жте': 'ї' is always [ji].

examples.source: Where are the eggs? They're on the table.

culture.title: Borscht, varenyky and recipes
culture.text:
Borscht, 'борщ', is a soup of beets, cabbage, potatoes, carrots and onion, usually cooked with meat, and it is the dish Ukrainians name first when they talk about their food. There is no single recipe. Every region and almost every family cooks it in its own way, and many people say that the right borscht is the one their mother or grandmother makes. In 2022 UNESCO inscribed the culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking on its list of intangible cultural heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.

Borscht is served hot with 'смета́на', a thick sour cream, and often with 'пампу́шки', small soft bread rolls brushed with garlic and oil. In spring many families also cook 'зеле́ний борщ', green borscht, made with sorrel instead of beets.

'Варе́ники' are dumplings of a simple dough of flour, water and often an egg, boiled in water; their name comes from 'вари́ти'. The most common fillings are:

- potatoes with fried onion
- 'сир', the fresh curd cheese
- cabbage
- cherries, in summer

Written Ukrainian recipes often give their steps in the 'ви' form of the imperative, mostly perfective: 'Поми́йте буря́к. Порі́жте цибу́лю. Дода́йте сіль.' A grandmother teaching at the stove speaks to her grandchild with 'ти' and rarely measures anything. She cooks 'на о́ко', literally 'on eye', which means by eye.

paragraphs.target: Споча́тку поми́йте карто́плю й зварі́ть її́. Порі́жте цибу́лю й посма́жте її́ на олі́ї. Не сма́жте її́ до́вго.
paragraphs.source: First wash the potatoes and boil them. Cut up the onion and fry it in oil. Don't fry it for long.
paragraphs.source_literal: First wash potatoes and boil them. Cut-up onion and fry it on oil. Not fry it long.

paragraphs.target: Зміша́йте карто́плю з цибу́лею й дода́йте тро́хи со́лі.
paragraphs.source: Mix the potatoes with the onion and add a little salt.
paragraphs.source_literal: Mix potatoes with onion and add a-little of-salt.

paragraphs.target: По́тім зміша́йте бо́рошно, одне́ яйце́, скля́нку води́ й тро́хи со́лі.
paragraphs.source: Then mix the flour, one egg, a glass of water and a little salt.
paragraphs.source_literal: Then mix flour, one egg, glass of-water and a-little of-salt.

paragraphs.target: Зробі́ть варе́ники й варі́ть їх у воді́ п’ять хвили́н. Ї́жте їх зі смета́ною!
paragraphs.source: Make the varenyky and boil them in water for five minutes. Eat them with sour cream!
paragraphs.source_literal: Make varenyky and boil them in water five of-minutes. Eat them with sour-cream!

questions.prompt: What does the recipe say to do with the onion?
choices: Cut it up and fry it in oil
questions.explanation: 'Порі́жте цибу́лю й посма́жте її́ на олі́ї': cut up the onion and fry it in oil. Later it is mixed with the potatoes.

choices: Flour, one egg, a glass of water and a little salt
questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists 'бо́рошно, одне́ яйце́, скля́нку води́ й тро́хи со́лі'. The potatoes and onion are the filling.

questions.prompt: How long are the varenyky boiled?
questions.explanation: 'Варі́ть їх у воді́ п’ять хвили́н': boil them in water for five minutes. The imperfective 'варі́ть' goes with a length of time.

exercises.prompt: Match the cooking verbs with their meanings
Match the ingredients with their English names
Which word is the 'ти' imperative of 'чита́ти'?
exercises.explanation: The stem 'чита-' ends in a vowel, so the imperative ends in '-й': 'чита́й'. 'Чита́єш' and 'чита́ють' are present forms.
'Дава́й' with an imperfective infinitive proposes doing something together. Here it does not mean 'give', because a second verb follows.
'Да́ти' has an irregular imperative: 'дай' for 'ти', 'да́йте' for 'ви'.
'Поми́ють' has a stem that ends in a vowel, so the imperative ends in '-й': 'поми́й'. The perfective fits one specific job.

exercises.prompt: Why is the imperative of 'писа́ти' 'пиши́', with '-и'?
choices: The stem 'пиш-' ends in a vowel.
The stem 'пиш-' ends in a consonant, and the 'я' form 'пишу́' is stressed on the ending.
The 'ти' form 'пи́шеш' is stressed on the stem.
exercises.explanation: After a consonant, '-и' is added when the 'я' form is stressed on the ending. The stress of the 'ти' form does not decide it: 'пи́шеш' has it on the stem, but 'пишу́' has it on the ending.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the 'ви' imperative of 'рі́зати'?
exercises.explanation: 'Рі́жу' is stressed on the stem, so the 'ти' form has no ending, 'ріж', and the 'ви' form adds '-те': 'рі́жте'. 'Рі́жете' is the present, 'you cut'.

exercises.prompt: Which is the imperative of 'пи́ти' for people you call 'ви'?
exercises.explanation: 'Пи́ти' has an irregular imperative: 'пий', 'пи́йте'. 'П’єте́' is the present for 'ви', and 'п’ють' the present for 'вони́'.

exercises.hint_source: Boil the varenyky for five minutes, said to several people. (вари́ти)
exercises.explanation: 'Варю́' is stressed on the ending, so the 'ти' form is 'вари́', and for 'ви' the 'и' becomes 'і': 'варі́ть'. The imperfective goes with a length of time.
'Говорю́' is stressed on the ending, so the imperative is 'говори́', and for 'ви' 'говорі́ть'. An instruction about how to do something takes the imperfective.

exercises.hint_source: Sam, don't eat the bread now. (ї́сти)
exercises.explanation: 'Ї́сти' has an irregular imperative: 'їж', 'ї́жте'. A command with 'не' takes the imperfective.

exercises.prompt: A recipe says 'Дода́йте сіль.' Why is the perfective 'дода́ти' used?
choices: It is one specific act that should be done and finished.
exercises.explanation: Each step of a recipe is one act with a result, so it takes the perfective. General advice and invitations take the imperfective.

exercises.prompt: Why does a host say 'Бері́ть, будь ла́ска.' with the imperfective?
choices: It invites guests to help themselves, and a perfective would sound like an order.
The verb 'бра́ти' has no perfective partner.
Only imperfective verbs have an imperative.
exercises.explanation: Invitations take the imperfective. 'Бра́ти' has the perfective partner 'взя́ти', and 'Візьмі́ть ка́ву.' tells someone to take the coffee.
After 'дава́й' an imperfective verb is in the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Дава́йте ___ ма́мі пода́рунок.' (Let's buy Mom a present.)?
exercises.explanation: After 'дава́йте' a perfective verb is in its future 'ми' form: 'ку́пимо'. 'Купі́ть' is the imperative for 'ви', and 'купи́ли' is a past form.
'Неха́й' or the shorter 'хай' with the 'вона́' form of a verb says what someone else should do.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'стань' end in a soft sign, but 'ріж' does not?
choices: The soft sign marks the stress.
'Стань' is the form for several people.
The 'н' at the end of 'стань' is soft, and 'ж' is never followed by the soft sign.
exercises.explanation: An imperative with no ending ends in the last consonant of the stem. 'Д', 'т', 'з', 'с', 'ц', 'л' and 'н' are soft there and take the soft sign; 'ж' cannot be soft.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the plural of 'яйце́'?
exercises.explanation: The plural is 'я́йця', with the stress moved to the first syllable. 'Яйце́м' is the instrumental singular and 'яйці́' the locative singular.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, what does Halyna tell Sam to do first?
choices: Wash the beet, the carrots and the potatoes
exercises.explanation: The meat is already in the saucepan, and Halyna says 'Поми́й буря́к, мо́ркву й карто́плю.' The garlic goes in at the end.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why does Olena say 'не бери́ цю' but then 'візьми́ вели́ку'?
choices: She speaks to two different people.
A command with 'не' takes the imperfective, and a request for one act takes the perfective.
'Бери́' is for a small spoon and 'візьми́' for a big one.
exercises.explanation: 'Бра́ти' and 'взя́ти' are one aspect pair. The negative command uses the imperfective 'бери́', and the request to take the big spoon uses the perfective 'візьми́'.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, when should Bohdan give the bill?
exercises.explanation: Andrii says 'Раху́нок дава́йте пі́сля ка́ви. Неха́й вони́ відпочива́ють.' Here 'дава́йте' simply means 'give'.

exercises.prompt_source: Wash the carrots and the beet.
Let Taras cut up the bread.
Add the cabbage to the saucepan. (said to several people)
exercises.explanation: 'Дода́ти' is built from 'да́ти', so its imperative is 'дода́й', and for 'ви' 'дода́йте'. A direction takes 'в' and the accusative, 'в' after a vowel.
'Дава́й' or 'дава́йте' takes a perfective verb in its future 'ми' form, 'зро́бимо', or an imperfective infinitive, 'роби́ти'.

exercises.prompt_source: Don't fry the fish for long. (said to a friend)
exercises.explanation: A command with 'не' takes the imperfective 'сма́жити'. 'Сма́жу' is stressed on the stem, so the 'ти' form has no ending: 'смаж'.
'Неха́й' or 'хай' takes the 'вона́' form, here the perfective future 'зро́бить', for one act.
